summary:
Radiation sensors measure exposure, but exposure alone cannot explain how an astronaut’s cells respond. BioShield-X bridges this gap through a working health monitoring software prototype connecting radiation data, molecular biomarkers, and mitochondrial protection research.

Using published NASA Artemis I measurements, our software calculates a 53.3% lower peak absorbed dose rate at Orion’s storm-shelter detector than at its crew-cabin detector. The prototype combines NASA OSDR resources with automated CSV analysis, interactive visualization, simulated biomarker monitoring, rule-based alerts, and simulated offline logging.

Our software-first approach requires no new hardware for the prototype, with future integration leveraging existing radiation detectors and onboard qPCR capabilities.

With over 290 ISS visitors from 26 countries, our potential customers include space agencies and commercial space operators. Future expansion targets aviation, healthcare, and occupational radiation research, subject to validation. Institutional licensing represents a potential commercialization pathway.

BioShield-X goes beyond environmental monitoring to support personalized biological research and future protective strategies.

details:
BioShield-X | Beyond Radiation. Within the Cell.

Problem & Scientific Motivation

Space radiation represents a major challenge for long-duration human spaceflight. Although conventional radiation monitoring systems quantify environmental exposure, radiation measurements alone cannot determine individual cellular responses or mitochondrial dysfunction.

BioShield-X addresses this gap by connecting space radiation monitoring, molecular biology, and mitochondria-targeted protection research through an interactive health monitoring software prototype.

Our Solution & How It Works

BioShield-X provides four integrated modules:

  • Health Monitor: Interactive visualization of radiation exposure and simulated molecular biomarkers, personal baseline comparisons, and rule-based review alerts.
  • NASA Evidence: Analysis of published radiation measurements, scientific research, and CSV data import.
  • Mission Log: Local recording and simulation of communication interruptions and reconnection.
  • Knowledge Guide: Scientific resources and interactive learning about radiation, mitochondrial health, biomarkers, and emerging biological protection research.

The software follows four stages: data collection, preparation, computational analysis, and visualization.

NASA Data & Quantifiable Results

Using published Artemis I HERA measurements of 287 and 134 μGy/min, BioShield-X calculates a 53.3% lower peak absorbed dose rate at the storm-shelter detector compared with the crew-cabin detector during a specific radiation-belt passage.

The project also draws on NASA OSDR study OSD-343 and published research involving 14 astronauts, supporting the investigation of cell-free mitochondrial DNA (cf-mtDNA) as a potential cellular stress biomarker.

Published research on SS-31 and cardiolipin provides a foundation for exploring mitochondria-targeted protection. However, its effectiveness against space radiation in astronauts remains unproven.

Innovation & Creativity

Unlike conventional exposure-monitoring approaches, BioShield-X introduces a separate molecular research layer that connects environmental monitoring with cellular-response evidence and future biological protection strategies.

Its originality lies in bridging space medicine, biotechnology, molecular biology, and software development within one research-oriented platform.

Technical Development & Feasibility

The working browser-based prototype was developed using HTML, CSS, JavaScript, CSV processing, descriptive statistics, and rule-based computational analysis.

The current prototype requires no additional hardware. Future development could leverage existing radiation detectors and onboard laboratory capabilities, such as NASA’s WetLab-2 qPCR research platform.

The prototype distinguishes published measurements from synthetic demonstration data and considers communication limitations, missing values, scientific uncertainty, accessibility, and future data privacy requirements.

Target Users & Market Opportunity

Primary users include astronauts, space medicine teams, space agencies, and commercial spaceflight operators.

Following appropriate validation, potential expansion could include aviation, healthcare, radiation research laboratories, and occupational health institutions.

Institutional software licensing, research partnerships, and integration with existing monitoring systems represent potential commercialization pathways.

Future Development & Intended Impact

Future milestones include integrating radiation sensor feeds, validating molecular biomarkers, developing predictive analytics using matched datasets, and establishing research partnerships to investigate mitochondrial protection.

BioShield-X is currently a research prototype, not a validated medical device or treatment system.

Our long-term vision is to advance space healthcare from measuring environmental exposure toward understanding individual biological responses and informing future protective strategies.

Monitor exposure. Understand the cell. Explore protection.
